title: The QMD File
text: A .qmd file is a plain text file combining Markdown for prose and code chunks for computation. This chapter covers the options that give you precise control over how code runs and how content is shown.

title: The QMD File
text:
Code chunk options
By default, Quarto shows both the code and its output. Chunk options let you override this — hiding code in a final report, adding captions, or skipping slow computations — without changing the logic of the code itself.
Every option is written as a #| comment at the top of the chunk. The chunk below runs print("Hello!") but hides the source code and suppresses warnings:
```{.python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: true
#| warning: false
print("Hello!")
```






NoteWhy {.python} instead of {python}?



In Quarto, curly braces without a dot — {python} — tell the engine to execute that block as Python code. This is what you want in your actual document, but in a tutorial like this one we only want to show the syntax without triggering execution.
Adding a dot — {.python} — switches the block to display-only: Quarto still applies Python syntax highlighting, but never runs the code. Alternatively, wrapping the entire example in a four-backtick ````markdown fence achieves the same effect.
In your own .qmd files, always use {python} (no dot) so the chunk actually runs.



Option reference








Option
Values
What it controls




echo
true / false / fenced
Show the source code


eval
true / false
Actually run the code


output
true / false / asis
Show the output


warning
true / false
Show warnings


error
true / false
Show errors (instead of stopping)


include
true / false
Include chunk at all (shorthand for echo+output: false)


code-fold
true / false
Collapse code into a toggle


code-summary
string
Label for the fold toggle


fig-cap
string
Caption for figures


fig-align
left / center / right
Figure alignment


label
string (must start with fig- or tbl-)
ID for cross-referencing





Common combinations
These three patterns cover most everyday use cases:


Hide code, show output
#| echo: false
The code runs silently — readers see only the result. Ideal for polished reports.

Show code, don’t run
#| eval: false
Useful for illustrative examples or code that would fail in the current environment.

Collapsible code block
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
Keeps the page clean while still letting curious readers expand the source.

title: The QMD File
text:
Global chunk defaults
Repeating the same options on every single chunk is tedious and error-prone. Set defaults once in _quarto.yml — they apply to every chunk in the project, and you only override where needed:


_quarto.yml

execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false

title: The QMD File
text:
Conditional content
Sometimes you need different text for different audiences or output formats — a simplified explanation for beginners and extra detail for intermediates, or an interactive widget in HTML that simply doesn’t exist in PDF.






TipShowing code examples inside Markdown



To display a code chunk without executing it, either wrap it in a four-backtick ````markdown fence, or use {.python} (with a dot) instead of {python}. Without the dot, Quarto treats the block as executable.



Profile-based content
Profiles are defined in _quarto.yml. Quarto evaluates them at render time — the .qmd source stays the same for every audience.


Markdown
::: {.content-visible when-profile="int"}
This paragraph only appears in the **intermediate** profile.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-profile="beg"}
This is hidden in the beginner profile, visible everywhere else.
:::

What happens
Rendering with quarto render --profile int includes only blocks tagged when-profile="int". Blocks tagged when-profile="beg" are hidden.
This lets you maintain a single source file for multiple audience levels without duplicating content.




Format-based content


Markdown
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
This only appears in HTML output.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
This only appears in PDF output.
:::

What happens
Quarto checks the output format at render time. Only the matching block is included — the rest is silently dropped.
Use this to embed interactive HTML elements (plots, widgets) while providing a static alternative for PDF.

title: The QMD File
text:
Cross-referencing
Cross-references let you write @fig-sine in prose and have Quarto automatically produce “Figure 1” — with a hyperlink in HTML and the correct number even if figures are reordered.

Figures


Markdown
```{.python}
#| label: fig-sine
#| fig-cap: "A plot of sin(x)"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 200)
plt.plot(x, np.sin(x))
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-sine, the sine function...

What happens
The label option registers the figure; fig-cap sets the caption. Writing @fig-sine in prose becomes a clickable “Figure 1” link in HTML and the correct number in PDF — Quarto handles the counting automatically.
Labels for figures must start with fig-.








Note



Reminder: Use {python} instead of {.python} in your own document — only the dot-version is used here to prevent execution in this tutorial.




Tables


Markdown
```{.python}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics"
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1,2,3], "y": [4,5,6]})
df
```

The values in @tbl-data show...

What happens
Works the same as figures — @tbl-data becomes “Table 1” wherever you write it. Labels for tables must start with tbl-.








Note



Reminder: Use {python} instead of {.python} in your own document




Sections


Markdown
## Introduction {#sec-intro}

As described in @sec-intro...

What happens
Adding {#sec-intro} to any heading makes it referenceable. @sec-intro becomes “Section 1” with a link in HTML. Section labels must start with sec-.








TipLabel naming rules




Figure labels must start with fig-
Table labels must start with tbl-
Section labels must start with sec-

title: The QMD File
text:
Custom divs and spans
CSS classes applied to a block let you style or target content without editing your stylesheet from within the .qmd file. Quarto passes the class straight through to the HTML output.


Markdown
::: {.my-class}
This block gets the `my-class` CSS class.
:::
For inline styling, use a span:
This word is [highlighted]{.my-highlight} in the text.

Output

This block gets the my-class CSS class.

This word is highlighted in the text.



Built-in Bootstrap utility classes
These work out of the box without any custom CSS:



Class
Effect




.text-center
Centre-align text


.text-muted
Grey text


.fw-bold
Bold text


.border
Add a border


.bg-light
Light background


.p-3
Add padding


.mt-4
Add top margin





Markdown
::: {.border .p-3 .bg-light}
This box has a border, padding, and a light background — no custom CSS needed.
:::

Output

This box has a border, padding, and a light background — no custom CSS needed.

title: The QMD File
text:
Callout blocks
Callouts draw attention to important information without breaking prose flow. Quarto renders them as styled boxes with an icon — use them for tips, warnings, or critical notes.


Markdown
::: {.callout-note}
## Optional title
Informational note.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
Practical advice.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Something to watch out for.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Critical information.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
Proceed carefully.
:::

Output






NoteOptional title



Informational note.








Tip



Practical advice.








Warning



Something to watch out for.








Important



Critical information.








Caution



Proceed carefully.




Add collapse="true" to make a callout collapsible — readers expand it on demand:


Markdown
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Click to expand
Hidden detail.
:::

Output






NoteClick to expand





Hidden detail.

title: Extensions
text:
This chapter covers the extensions used in this tutorial. Most extensions are installed once per project with quarto add <name> — the files land in _extensions/ and should be committed to git.
Extensions can be enabled globally in _quarto.yml or per page in the frontmatter:

title: Extensions
text:
quizdown — interactive quizzes
Install: quarto add parmsam/quizdown
Source: (Sauer 2023) — github.com/parmsam/quarto-quizdown

# Which file controls global project settings in Quarto?

1. [x] `_quarto.yml`
1. [ ] `index.qmd`
1. [ ] `styles.css`

# Select all valid Quarto output formats.

- [x] HTML
- [x] PDF
- [x] Word (.docx)
- [ ] Excel (.xlsx)

# Put the Quarto render pipeline in the correct order.

1. Parse `.qmd` source
2. Execute code chunks
3. Convert Markdown to HTML/PDF
4. Apply theme and styles


SettingsQuestion typesImages & code


Global quiz settings go inside a --- block at the top of the quiz:
```{quizdown}
---
shuffleAnswers: true    # default: true — randomise answer order
shuffleQuestions: false # default: false — randomise question order
---
```






Tip



shuffleAnswers: true is the default — answers are shuffled unless you explicitly set it to false.




Single choice — exactly one correct answer:
```{quizdown}
# What is 2 + 2?
1. [ ] 3
1. [x] 4
1. [ ] 5
```
Multiple choice — more than one correct answer:
```{quizdown}
# Which of these are programming languages?
- [x] Python
- [ ] Quarto
- [x] R
- [x] JavaScript
```
Ordering — put these items in the correct order:
```{quizdown}
# Put the Quarto render pipeline in the correct order.

1. Parse `.qmd` source
2. Execute code chunks
3. Convert Markdown to HTML/PDF
4. Apply theme and styles
```


Include an image in a question:
```{quizdown}
# What does this logo belong to?
![](https://quarto.org/quarto.png)
1. [x] Quarto
1. [ ] RMarkdown
```
Include inline code in answers:
```{quizdown}
# Which chunk option hides the source code?
1. [x] `echo: false`
1. [ ] `eval: false`
1. [ ] `output: false`
```

title: Extensions
section: Pyodide — live Python in the browser
text:
Pyodide — live Python in the browser
Install: quarto add coatless-quarto/pyodide
Source: (Droettboom et al. 2021) — github.com/coatless-quarto/pyodide

ExampleSetup & optionsvs. regular Python



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Enable per page:
---
filters:
  - coatless-quarto/pyodide
---
Or globally in _quarto.yml (applies to all pages):
filters:
  - coatless-quarto/pyodide
Per-chunk options:
```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true     # run automatically on page load
#| read-only: true   # reader cannot edit the code
print("Auto-runs, cannot be changed.")
```






{python}
{pyodide-python}




Runs at
Render time
Read time (in browser)


Reader can edit
No
Yes


Needs Python installed
Yes (author)
No (reader)


Output baked into HTML
Yes
No — computed live









WarningPackage availability



Pyodide runs in WebAssembly. Most pure-Python packages work (numpy, pandas, matplotlib) but packages with C extensions may not be available.






pyodide-interaktiv — the fork this tutorial runs on
Install: copy the folder — not published yet (see the Install tab)
Source: (Erasmus CTM, n.d.c) — github.com/Erasmus-CTM/Pyodide-interaktiv
pyodide-interaktiv is a rework of coatless-quarto/pyodide that runs Python in a Web Worker instead of on the browser’s main thread. The cell syntax is identical — {pyodide-python} with the same #| options — so pages swap between the two by changing one line in filters:. What the worker buys you is everything below.






NoteThe cells on this page use the fork



Every {pyodide-python} example on this page — including the one above — is executed by pyodide-interaktiv, because only one Pyodide extension can be active per page.



What’s newShared stateinput()Plots & animationAI feedbackOptionsInstall











coatless-quarto/pyodide
pyodide-interaktiv




Python runs on
Main thread
Web Worker


Page during a long run
Frozen
Stays responsive


Runaway loop (while True:)
Tab is stuck
Stop button cancels it


input()
Not supported
Real, blocking input()


Animations
Static image
Interactive player


AI feedback
—
Feedback button on every cell


Interface language
English
en, de, sv, no/nb, da



The language is read from Quarto’s own lang: key, so a multilingual project needs no extra setting — see Multilanguage Projects.


All cells on a page share one Python session — this is true of the base extension as well — so a later cell can reuse anything an earlier one defined:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Cells that should run before the reader touches anything use context: setup; cells whose result is shown but whose code is hidden use context: output.


A cell can stop and wait for typed input without freezing the page:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Warninginput() needs cross-origin isolation



Blocking input relies on SharedArrayBuffer, which browsers only hand out to cross-origin-isolated pages. A service worker shipped with the extension sets the required headers automatically on your own domain. Learning platforms such as Moodle usually block service workers — there input() is simply unavailable and the page says so. Everything else keeps working.




With the pyodide-interaktiv extension Animations become plotable.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
A live version of this is on the Code page of the Example Page.






TipSpeed is interval, not frames



interval is the delay between frames in milliseconds — 33 ms is roughly 30 fps. Matplotlib’s default of 200 ms looks visibly choppy. frames only sets how many frames are drawn, so raising it makes the animation longer, not smoother. Every frame is pre-rendered and embedded, so long animations cost render time and page weight.


For special cases, zeige_animation(ani, format="gif") and zeige_animation(ani, fps=30) control format and frame rate directly.


Every interactive cell gets a Feedback button that sends the current code plus its output to a language model and shows the answer under the cell. A ⚙ icon at the top of the document opens the settings panel:







Field
Meaning




Provider template
fills in base URL and an example model for OpenRouter, Cerebras, Groq, OpenAI or Ollama


Base URL
API endpoint, e.g. https://openrouter.ai/api/v1


API key
stays in the browser only, never in the rendered page


Model
free text; Fetch models lists the provider’s models, free ones by default


Feedback mode
Direct API or Copy prompt


Storage
localStorage (persistent) or sessionStorage (per tab)



Without an API key, Copy prompt mode produces a ready-to-paste prompt for ChatGPT, Claude and the like — no account needed for the reader.
Hints get more concrete with each click on the same cell (1 = nudge, 2 = names the problem, 3 = describes the solution in words — never finished code). Turn it off with feedback-hints: false.


page.qmd

pyodide:
  feedback: true            # show Feedback buttons (default: true)
  feedback-storage: local   # local | session
  feedback-hints: true      # progressive hints (default: true)







Important



The API key lives in the reader’s browser. Never put a key into the .qmd — it would be published with the site.




Per cell:



Option
Default
Description




context
interactive
interactive, output or setup


read-only
false
editor is locked (no feedback button)


autorun
—
true: run once Pyodide has started


label
—
unique cell ID


classes
—
extra CSS classes


fig-cap
—
caption for plots


fig-width / fig-height
7 / 5
plot size in inches



Per document:


page.qmd

pyodide:
  packages: [numpy, pandas]   # installed at startup via micropip
  base-url: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/v0.27.2/
  show-startup-message: true
  lang: de                    # interface language (default: en)

Packages that only appear in an import are fetched on demand, so packages: is for the ones you want ready before the first run. requests/urllib3 are shimmed, so pd.read_csv(url) works.








ImportantNot yet quarto add-able



pyodide-interaktiv, py-exercise and math-exercise are not in the public extension registry yet — only coatless-quarto/pyodide is. Until they are published, vendor them by hand.


① Copy the extension folder
Copy _extensions/Erasmus-CTM/pyodide-interaktiv/ from this project into your own project’s _extensions/ folder.
② Reference it by folder name


page.qmd

---
title: "My Page"
format: html
filters:
  - pyodide-interaktiv
---

A vendored extension needs no quarto add step, and it is referenced by folder name only — without the Erasmus-CTM/ prefix that a registry install would add.






WarningOne Pyodide extension per page



coatless-quarto/pyodide and pyodide-interaktiv both claim {pyodide-python}. Listing both in filters: loads two runtimes and breaks the cells — pick one.


Two more limits worth knowing: embed-resources does not work (Pyodide ships WebAssembly binaries), and navigating to another page of the project reloads the runtime.

title: Extensions
section: py-exercise — editable exercises with hidden tests
text:
py-exercise — editable exercises with hidden tests
Install: copy the folder — not published yet
Source: (Erasmus CTM, n.d.b) — github.com/Erasmus-CTM/Py-Exercise






NoteWorks on its own



py-exercise no longer needs a Pyodide extension next to it. On its own it loads Pyodide and the Monaco editor from a CDN when the reader first runs an exercise:


exercises.qmd — standalone

filters:
  - py-exercise

If the page does have a Pyodide extension, list it first — py-exercise then reuses that runtime instead of booting a second one:


page.qmd — combined

filters:
  - pyodide-interaktiv
  - py-exercise




ExampleSyntaxOptionsRestricting solutionsSubmission



  
    Please enable JavaScript to load the interactive exercise.
  




```{py-exercise}
def my_function(x):
    """Docstring shown to the reader."""
    # Student fills this in
    pass

## TESTS ##
assert my_function(2) == 4, "Feedback shown on failure"
assert my_function(0) == 0
```
Rules: 1. Write the function stub with a docstring at the top. 2. ## TESTS ## is the separator — everything below is hidden from the reader. 3. Each assert statement’s message becomes the feedback shown on test failure.






Tip



Write assertion messages as if you are talking to the student: "my_function(2) should return 4 — did you multiply correctly?"




Per cell:








Option
Default
Description




label
py-exercise-N
unique exercise ID


caption
—
title above the exercise


forbidden-imports
—
comma-separated imports the solution may not use


forbidden-keywords
—
comma-separated Python keywords the solution may not use


show-test-hints
true
show the assertion message when a test fails



Per document — the same keys, applied to every exercise on the page:


exercises.qmd

py-exercise:
  forbidden-imports: [os, sys, subprocess]
  forbidden-keywords: [for, while, sorted]
  show-test-hints: true
  lang: de                   # interface language (default: en)



Forbidden constructs are checked before the code runs — a violation is reported instead of a test result:
```{py-exercise}
#| caption: Fibonacci, recursively
#| forbidden-keywords: for, while
def fib(n):
    pass

## TESTS ##
assert fib(6) == 8,   "fib(6) should be 8"
assert fib(10) == 55, "fib(10) should be 55"
```
Typical uses: banning for/while to force recursion or comprehensions, banning sorted to make students write the algorithm, banning os/sys/subprocess in an open learning environment.


With submission: true the page gets a header asking for a student ID and a quiz ID. Once the tests pass, the student can download the result as a JSON file, XOR-encoded with submission-key and Base64-wrapped so the raw results are not readable without the key.


exercises.qmd

py-exercise:
  submission: true
  submission-key: "sose25-quiz1"







Warning



The key is in the rendered page, so this deters casual tampering — it is not real cryptography. Treat it as a convenience for collecting results, not as an exam-grade safeguard.

title: Extensions
section: math-exercise — symbolic answers checked with SymPy
text:
math-exercise — symbolic answers checked with SymPy
Install: copy the folder — not published yet
Source: (Erasmus CTM, n.d.a) — github.com/Erasmus-CTM/Math-Exercise
Where py-exercise checks code, math-exercise checks an answer. Students type a mathematical expression into an input field and it is compared with SymPy — so any equivalent form counts as correct.






NoteWorks on its own



Like py-exercise, math-exercise loads Pyodide and SymPy itself on the first Check click if no Pyodide extension is present. When one is, list it first:


page.qmd

filters:
  - pyodide-interaktiv
  - math-exercise




ExampleSyntaxOptionsChecking modesQuestion poolsInput help & feedback



Area of a circle


A circle has radius $r = 3$. Give its area exactly (use `pi`):

$A =$ 

  ✓ Check
  ⓘ Input help
  
    💬 Feedback
    ⚙
  





pi*9, 9*pi and 3**2*pi are all accepted — they are the same expression.


```{math-exercise}
#| label: my-exercise
#| caption: Exercise title
#| vars: x
Question text with an input field: _[correct_answer]
```
The answer inside [...] is a SymPy expression, e.g. pi * 9 or x**2 + 2*x + 1. Three field widths are available:



Marker
Width
Element




_[answer]
narrow (~10 characters)
<input>


__[answer]
medium (~20 characters)
<input>


___[answer]
wide, two lines
<textarea>



Several fields in one exercise are checked together on Check.





Option
Default
Description




label
math-exercise-N
unique exercise ID


caption
—
title above the exercise


vars
—
SymPy symbols, e.g. x, y, r


mode
equivalent
equivalent or exact


reject
—
expression to refuse even though it is correct


pool
false
treat the block as a pool of variants





page.qmd

math-exercise:
  lang: de     # interface language (default: en)







Important



Any symbol used in the answer has to be listed in vars — otherwise SymPy has no idea what x is meant to be.




equivalent (default) — accepts every mathematically equivalent form. For [pi * 9], all of pi*9, 9*pi and 3**2 * pi pass.
equivalent + reject — accepts equivalent forms except the one given. This is what makes simplification exercises work: the student cannot just retype the question.
```{math-exercise}
#| vars: x
#| mode: equivalent
#| reject: (x+1)**2
Expand: $(x+1)^2 =$ __[x**2 + 2*x + 1]
```
→ (x+1)^2 is refused, x^2 + 2x + 1 is accepted.
exact — accepts only SymPy’s canonical form of the answer. Use it when one specific notation is required.


With pool: true and --- as a separator, one block holds several variants. Each page visit picks one at random and keeps it for the session; a ↻ button loads a different one.
```{math-exercise}
#| label: circle-pool
#| caption: Area of a circle
#| vars: r
#| pool: true
Radius r = 3 cm. $A =$ _[pi*9] cm²

---

Radius r = 5 cm. $A =$ _[pi*25] cm²

---

Radius r = 7 cm. $A =$ _[pi*49] cm²
```
All variants share the same options (vars, mode, reject).


Each exercise has a collapsible input help listing the notation students need — x^2 or x**2, sqrt(x), root(x, n), pi, E, Abs(x), oo, integrate(f, x), diff(f, x).
The Feedback button works like the one in pyodide-interaktiv: same settings dialog, same providers, same progressive hint levels — and credentials entered once in localStorage are reused across all pages of the project.

text:
This is a Tutorial for using Quarto in a creating context.

If you never saw a Quarto page before click here!
If you want to learn how to create something with Quarto click here!
If you already know how to create Quarto Documents and want to become better click here!

title: Cheatsheet
text: A quick reference for everything covered in this section.

title: Cheatsheet
text:
YAML — _quarto.yml options

Project
project:
  type: website       # website | book | manuscript | default
  output-dir: docs    # where rendered files go


Execute (global code defaults)
execute:
  echo: true          # show source code
  eval: true          # run the code
  warning: false      # hide warnings
  error: false        # hide errors
  freeze: auto        # auto | true | false


Format
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    theme: cosmo
    theme:
      - cosmo
      - custom.scss
    code-fold: true
    code-tools: true
    number-sections: false
  pdf:
    toc: true
    documentclass: article
    geometry: margin=2.5cm
  docx:
    toc: true


Website
website:
  title: "My Site"
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: "Home"
        href: index.qmd
      - text: "External"
        href: https://example.com
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/your/repo
  sidebar:
    - id: my-sidebar
      style: docked        # docked | floating
      contents:
        - href: page.qmd
          text: Page Title
        - section: "Group"
          contents:
            - href: sub.qmd
              text: Sub-page


Profiles
profile:
  default: web
  group: [web, print, de, en]

title: Cheatsheet
Multilanguage Projects
text: Quarto does not have a built-in translation system, but profiles make it straightforward to build a project that serves content in multiple languages — each profile renders to its own output folder.

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Project structure
my-project/
├── _quarto.yml
├── _quarto-de.yml
├── _quarto-en.yml
├── de/
│   ├── index.qmd
│   └── chapter1.qmd
├── en/
│   ├── index.qmd
│   └── chapter1.qmd
└── docs/
    ├── de/
    └── en/

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Step 1 — Profile group


_quarto.yml

project:
  type: website

profile:
  default: en
  group: [en, de]

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Step 2 — Per-language config files


_quarto-en.yml

project:
  output-dir: docs/en
  render:
    - en/*.qmd

website:
  title: "My Project"
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: "Home"
        href: en/index.qmd
      - text: "🇩🇪 Deutsch"
        href: "de/index.html"    # ← links to DE start page only



_quarto-de.yml

project:
  output-dir: docs/de
  render:
    - de/*.qmd

website:
  title: "Mein Projekt"
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: "Startseite"
        href: de/index.qmd
      - text: "🇬🇧 English"
        href: "en/index.html"    # ← links to EN start page only

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Step 3 — Render each language






ImportantQuarto cannot render all profiles at once natively



quarto render only runs the default profile. You must render each profile separately:
quarto render --profile en
quarto render --profile de
Use a build script (like preview.py in this project) to automate this.

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Language switcher fix
Quarto’s navbar links point to the other language’s homepage — they cannot know which page the reader is currently on.
A Python post-processing script solves this: after rendering, it rewrites the language-switch link in every HTML file to point to the equivalent page in the other language.
This works as long as your source files have matching names across languages:
en/chapter1.qmd  →  docs/en/chapter1.html
de/chapter1.qmd  →  docs/de/chapter1.html
Add this to your build script after rendering:
import os, re

def fix_language_links(docs_dir, lang_pairs):
    """
    Rewrite language-switch hrefs to point to the equivalent page
    instead of the other language's homepage.

    lang_pairs: list of (from_lang, to_lang) tuples, e.g. [("en", "de"), ("de", "en")]
    """
    docs_path = os.path.abspath(docs_dir)

    for from_lang, to_lang in lang_pairs:
        lang_dir = os.path.join(docs_path, from_lang)
        if not os.path.isdir(lang_dir):
            continue
        for dirpath, _, filenames in os.walk(lang_dir):
            for filename in filenames:
                if not filename.endswith(".html"):
                    continue
                html_file = os.path.join(dirpath, filename)
                rel = os.path.relpath(html_file, lang_dir)
                # Compute the path to the equivalent page in the other language
                depth = len(rel.replace("\\", "/").split("/")) - 1
                prefix = "../" * depth
                equivalent = prefix + "../" + to_lang + "/" + rel.replace("\\", "/")

                with open(html_file, encoding="utf-8") as f:
                    content = f.read()
                # Replace the generic language-switch link
                new_content = content.replace(
                    f'href="{prefix}../{to_lang}/index.html"',
                    f'href="{equivalent}"'
                )
                if new_content != content:
                    with open(html_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                        f.write(new_content)

fix_language_links("docs", [("en", "de"), ("de", "en")])

title: Multilanguage Projects
section: Conditional content within a shared file
text:
Conditional content within a shared file
For small projects, you can maintain a single set of files and use conditional divs:
::: {.content-visible when-profile="en"}
Welcome to this tutorial.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="de"}
Willkommen zu diesem Tutorial.
:::






Warning



This approach works for small projects but becomes hard to maintain as content grows. For anything beyond a few pages, separate source folders (one per language) are strongly recommended.

title: Multilanguage Projects
text:
Shared content across languages
Files that don’t need translation (code examples, shared figures) can be included with Quarto’s include shortcode:
{{< include ../../shared/code-example.qmd >}}
Place shared files in a shared/ folder outside the language folders.

title: The YML File
text: The _quarto.yml file is the control centre of your Quarto project. Everything you set here applies globally — unless overridden in a specific .qmd file or profile.

title: The YML File
text:
Output formats
Quarto can render the same source to multiple formats at once:


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: cosmo
  pdf:
    toc: true
    documentclass: article
  docx:
    toc: true

Run all formats: quarto render Run one format: quarto render --to pdf






Tip



Any format option can be overridden per page in the .qmd file’s own YAML frontmatter.

title: The YML File
text:
Execute & freeze


_quarto.yml

execute:
  echo: true        # show source code
  eval: true        # run the code
  warning: false    # suppress warnings
  freeze: auto      # re-run only when source changes




freeze value
Behaviour




false
Always re-execute


true
Never re-execute — use cached output


auto
Re-execute only when the .qmd file changes



Frozen results are stored in _freeze/ — commit this folder so collaborators don’t need to re-run everything.






Warning



freeze: auto watches the .qmd file, not your data files. If you update a CSV but not the .qmd, delete the matching folder in _freeze/ to force a re-run.

title: The YML File
text:
Profiles
Profiles let you maintain multiple build variants — different audiences, languages, or formats — from one project.


_quarto.yml

profile:
  default: web
  group: [web, print]

Each profile has its own config file _quarto-<name>.yml that overrides or extends the root config:


_quarto-print.yml

project:
  output-dir: docs/print
format:
  pdf:
    toc: true

Render a specific profile:
quarto render --profile print






Tip



This entire tutorial is built with three profiles — beg, int, and exp — each with its own sidebar, navbar, and output folder.

title: The YML File
text:
Sidebar

Basic setup


_quarto.yml

website:
  sidebar:
    - id: my-sidebar
      style: docked       # docked | floating
      collapse-level: 1   # how many levels are expanded by default
      contents:
        - href: page.qmd
          text: "Page Title"



Sections — collapsible groups
Use section: to create collapsible groups in the sidebar. A section can have its own overview page (href) or just be a label:
contents:
  - section: "Chapter 1"          # label only, no page
    contents:
      - href: ch1/part1.qmd
        text: Part 1

  - section: "Chapter 2"
    href: ch2/index.qmd           # clicking the section title opens this page
    contents:
      - href: ch2/part1.qmd
        text: Part 1


Collapse level
collapse-level controls how many nesting levels are expanded when the page loads:



Value
Effect




1
Only top-level items visible, all sections collapsed


2
Top level and first-level sections expanded


3
Everything expanded



sidebar:
  collapse-level: 1   # start collapsed — reader expands what they need


Collapsible sidebar (hide/show)
To allow readers to collapse the sidebar entirely, use:


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    sidebar: true    # this is the default

For a floating sidebar that can be dismissed:
website:
  sidebar:
    style: floating
